alt: Two tests in order: factual causation, the but for test (R v White, where the victim died before the poison worked), then legal causation, an operating and substantial cause (R v Smith). Three cards show when the chain is not broken: the thin skull rule (Blaue), poor medical treatment unless palpably wrong or the wound is insignificant (Jordan, Cheshire), and a foreseeable escape (Roberts).
caption: Prove "but for" and an operating and substantial cause; the chain is rarely broken.

alt: Three OAPA 1861 offences with their mens rea: s 47 needs mens rea for the assault only, s 20 needs foresight of some harm and s 18 needs intention. Cards define direct intention (Mohan), oblique intention (Woollin) and subjective recklessness (Cunningham, R v G), then transferred malice (Latimer, but not Pembliton) and coincidence (Fagan).
caption: Similar actus reus, different mens rea: s 47, s 20 and s 18 are separated by the mental element.

alt: Five rows give the elements of theft with their sections and cases: dishonestly (s 2, Ivey test and the s 2 exceptions), appropriates (s 3, Morris and Gomez), property (s 4), belonging to another (s 5, including s 5(4)) and intention permanently to deprive (s 6, Lloyd on borrowing).
caption: Dishonesty, appropriation, property, belonging to another, intention to permanently deprive: ss 2 to 6.

alt: Duress of threats: a threat of death or serious injury, then the two-stage Graham test, subjective then objective. It is not available for murder (Howe) or attempted murder (Gotts) and is lost on voluntary association with criminals (Hasan); duress of circumstances uses the same test. Intoxication: voluntary is no defence to basic intent (Majewski); involuntary helps only if mens rea was not formed (Kingston, Hardie).
caption: Duress needs both Graham stages and never covers murder; intoxication rarely helps if intent was formed.

alt: Four sentence types stacked from most to least severe: custody (only where nothing less can be justified, may be suspended), community orders with requirements, fines set by seriousness and means, and conditional or absolute discharges. Below, the court considers seriousness, aggravating and mitigating factors, and up to one third off for an early guilty plea.
caption: Custody is the last resort; seriousness, aggravation, mitigation and plea set the level.

alt: The two routes to burglary: s 9(1)(a), entering as a trespasser with intent, complete on entry; and s 9(1)(b), committing an offence after entering as a trespasser. Four steps apply them to Owen: he is a trespasser, a garage is a building, he intended to steal so s 9(1)(a) is complete, and there is no robbery because nothing was stolen.
caption: Intent at the moment of entry completes s 9(1)(a); no theft means no robbery.
